The word trial carries one central idea: a test. Whether something is being judged, examined, or put through difficulty — a trial is always about determining something through a process. Keep this idea of testing in your mind, and every meaning of this word will make perfect sense.

1. A Legal Process in Court

This is the most well-known meaning. A trial is a formal process in a court of law where a judge (and sometimes a jury) listens to facts and evidence to decide whether a person is guilty or innocent of a crime.

Think of it as a structured, official test of the truth.

  • "The trial lasted six weeks."
  • "He was found not guilty at the end of the trial."
  • "She demanded a fair trial."

Key things that happen during a trial: lawyers argue, witnesses speak, evidence is shown, and a decision is reached. It's the legal system's way of testing whether an accusation is true or false.

2. A Test of Something (To See If It Works)

A trial is also a test you do before committing to something fully — to see if it works, performs well, or is suitable. This is very common in science, medicine, business, and everyday life.

  • "The company offered a free 30-day trial of their app."
  • "Scientists conducted a clinical trial of the new medicine."
  • "We ran a trial to see if the new system would work."

Here, nothing permanent has been decided yet. The trial is the discovery phase — you're testing before you fully trust or adopt something.

3. A Hardship or Difficult Experience

In a more emotional and personal sense, a trial refers to something that is painful, difficult, or challenging to go through — an experience that tests your strength, patience, or character.

  • "Raising three children alone was a great trial for her."
  • "He faced many trials in his early years."
  • "The loss of her job was a real trial."

Notice how this meaning also connects to the idea of being "tested" — but here, life itself is doing the testing, and you are the one being tested.

4. A Sports Selection Test

In sports, a trial (or trials) is a competitive test given to players or athletes to see if they are good enough to be selected for a team or squad.

  • "He went to the football trial hoping to impress the coach."
  • "She passed her athletics trials and made the national team."

Again, it's a test — this time of skill and ability.

These are very commonly used, so learning them is essential.

Trial and error — The process of learning by trying different things and learning from your failures until you succeed.

  • "He learned to cook mostly through trial and error."

On trial — Being formally judged in a court of law.

  • "The suspect is currently on trial for fraud."

Stand trial — To go through the legal process of being formally judged in court.

  • "She will stand trial next month."

Trial run — A practice attempt at something before doing it for real, to check that it works properly.

  • "Let's do a trial run of the presentation before the big day."

Trial period — A set amount of time during which something is tested before a final decision is made.

  • "The software comes with a 14-day trial period."

Trials and tribulations — A phrase meaning the many difficulties and sufferings a person faces in life. (Tribulations also means hardships.) Used together for emphasis.

  • "Despite all his trials and tribulations, he never gave up."

Clinical trial — A carefully controlled scientific test of a new medicine or medical treatment on human volunteers, done before it is approved for public use.

  • "The new cancer drug is currently in clinical trials."

Put on trial / Bring to trial — To formally take someone to court to be judged.

  • "The accused was brought to trial after months of investigation."

By trial — Through the process of testing.

  • "The best method was found by trial."

You might wonder: why does one word mean a courtroom process, and a product test, and a life hardship, and a sports selection? The answer is that all these meanings share the same soul — the idea of being tested or examined to reach a conclusion.

  • In a court trial, the truth is being tested.
  • In a product trial, the product's quality is being tested.
  • In a life trial, your strength and endurance are being tested.
  • In a sports trial, your ability is being tested.

Once you see that connecting thread, the word becomes very intuitive.

Trial as a noun means: a legal court process, a test of a product or idea, a difficult life experience, or a sports selection test. In every case, something or someone is being put through a process to reach a verdict, a conclusion, or a judgment. The word is often used in phrases like trial and error, on trial, trial run, and trials and tribulations.
